items.title: Pogačar’s Viral Booty Band Warm-Up Routine Might Just Be a Placebo
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Should cyclists warm up with mini bands? Why the placebo effect might outweigh any true muscle 'activation,' and how riders can make better use of glute bands.
items.lbText:
Tadej Pogačar made “booty bands” everybody’s favorite warm-up ritual when he was filmed twerking and squatting his way through a pre-race routine, bands around his knees.

But it turns out that these wildly popular pre-ride workouts might largely be a placebo .

Waddling, lunging, and squatting through a mini-band session before a ride doesn’t “activate your glutes” or prime you to push max power.

According to WorldTour experts, the power of glute bands might largely be in the mind.

“These mini band moves are beneficial, but it’s more from a pseudo-science perspective. Someone riders might feel like, ‘Oh, I’m doing something , I’m preparing myself to ride’ by doing them,” Jayco-AlUla physiotherapist Dan Guillemette told Velo .

“But in terms of actual performance, it’s really unlikely there’s any actual benefit.”

So how have mini-bands become one of sport’s most popular primers?

They’ve become no-brainers for WorldTour and triathlon pros, TikTok influencers, 4w/kg Velo writers [ ahem ], and everyone in between.

Here’s why mini band warm-ups might not be worth your time – unless you’re already doing them – and how to make better use of these wildly popular home workout tools.

Pogačar’s pre-race warm-up video was one of the viral cycling clips of 2025. The meme pages loved it.

The Instagram reel shows Pogačar and his teammate Juan Molano working through a series of mini band exercises ahead of a stage at the UAE Tour. Pogi’s now-famous “bum to the sky” hip opener was a particular highlight.

It was a rare behind-the-scenes glimpse at how pros prepare to push wild watts for hours on end.

Since then, clips of Matteo Jorgenson , Jonas Abrahamsen , and Remco Evenepoel doing similar routines have reinforced the thinking that a few minutes inside a mini band will push you to new performance peaks.

And unlike a set of Pogačar-approved 165mm cranks or an indoor trainer “heat suit,” there’s no expensive equipment, excess sweat, or annoying apps involved.

All you need is a $10 band from Walmart and one of the routines being pumped into your cycling social feed.

The big selling point of booty band routines for cyclists and endurance athletes?

That they waken your glutes from their slumber after too long being sat on. A few minutes pushing at a mini band will buzz your butt into “workout mode.”

Strength expert Chris Peden burst that bubble when he spoke to Velo .

Peden, the head of S&C at Decathlon CMA-CGM, said pros and amateurs alike have been fooled by a misapplication of the term “sleepy glutes.”

“These routines are always advertised as ‘you’ve got weak glutes, your glutes don’t work, or are ‘asleep.’ That’s the result of medical terms transferring to the performance world that don’t really apply,” Peden told Velo . “It’s a medical term from those who are extremely inactive, not somebody who does even a low level of training.

“And anyway, muscles don’t ‘switch on’ or ‘switch off,’” Peden continued. “Your neuromuscular system is always working. Your brain knows exactly what to recruit at any one time,” Peden said.

“A band workout does not make that signal ‘better’ or ‘cleaner,’ as some suggest. It’s unlikely to have any benefit at all.”

If you’re reading this post, you’re likely interested in bikes and maybe ride one every so often.

A second misconception? That squeezing some torque out of your glutes with an oversized elastic band will ready you for your 400-watt interval workout.

That’s founded in another misapplication, this time of the term “PAP.”

PAP, or Post Activation Potentiation, refers to the acute boost in muscular performance following a previous activity. A set of heavy back squats before attempting a maximum vertical jump is a common real-world application of PAP.

But sadly, a set of waddling “monster walks” won’t come close to delivering the muscular force or speed required for any meaningful PAP.

In the world’s biggest bike races, turbo trainers – not mini bands – are used to provide an effective potentiation.

These torture devices are wheeled out of team trucks ahead of time trials, hard uphill starts, or for those wanting to make the day’s early break. Riders work through a progressive build before a series of short submaximal efforts that fully stimulate the muscles for a fast racing start.

So, wait one sec. If the popular theories behind booty bands are a load of BS, why are they still so popular in the dialed-down, scientifically-backed WorldTour?

Even Peden admitted his own athletes on Decathlon CMA-CGM do them, even though he dismisses their direct impact on performance. Both he and Guillemette at Jayco-AlUla think that for many riders, the gains are all in the mind.

For many, workout bands became part of their pre-ride routine as juniors, either as a misguided warm-up tool or as a minimal dose of strength work.

“Psychologically, the placebo effect is massive,” Peden said. “Our riders still do them regardless of what we might say. They’ve been told to do it since they were 15 years old, and that it’s beneficial to them. So I can’t turn around to tell them to suddenly stop.

“They’re not doing any harm, but they’re not achieving anything meaningful as a supposed ‘activation,’” he continued. “If they’re proving some psychological benefit and riders believe they help, I’m not going to hold them back. However, I might try to suggest they include some more useful practices, instead – say, around mobility.”

Guillemette, who worked at Team Sky before he joined Jayco-AlUla, added that a band routine can also help riders transition out of inactivity.

They prime the mind and loosen the body.

“It’s really unlikely that there’s any benefit to using bands in terms of race performance,” Guillemette said.…

items.title: 11 Prime Day Cycling Deals Actually Worth Buying in 2026
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Navigating Amazon's cynical retail holiday is an exhausting chore. Here are 11 genuine 2026 discounts on cycling tech, smart trainers, and nutrition from Wahoo, Garmin, and GoPro that I recommend at full price.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Welcome to Velo Deals. We sift through the retail landscape to bring you deals worth paying attention to. It might be a discount or it might just be a product so good you should grab it. Either way, if it’s worth your time, you’ll see it here. If you’d like to see the rest of the category, check all our Velo Deals coverage.

Amazon Prime Day is perhaps the most cynical holiday of all time. Despite that, if you were going to buy something anyway, you might as well save money. I went looking for products I know and love that are also on sale. I managed to find 11 cycling Prime Day deals on gear I’d tell you to buy any day of the year, now offered for less. There’s a bit of a tech lean to Prime Day, so you will see that represented here, but I’ve got some cycling nutrition in the mix as well.

Wahoo bike computers are all about simplicity. They are simple to use but don’t skimp on what you need. The last piece of the puzzle Wahoo has lacked was self-training off the bike computer, and now there’s access to Wahoo and Coros training dashboards. The ELEMNT Bolt 3 is likely going to be my best budget bike computer in future best bike computer buying guides , and at 36% off, nothing else competes.

If you like to listen to music while you ride, the absolute best way to do it is with bone conduction headphones, and SHOKZ is the market leader. You can still hear what is happening around you, and on top of that, they can’t fall off, they’ve got tons of battery life, and if you want to stop your music, a single button press lets them disappear without having to stash them in a pocket.

The one challenge with bone conduction headphones is that they aren’t the best choice off the bike, and the mic performance is universally bad. If you are looking for something that will stay secure on the bike (use just a single earbud) and works well in regular life, then Apple users want the AirPods Pro 3. I’ve also tested these on a trainer with a fan at my face, and for the Apple ecosystem, this is what you want.

Winter is coming and that means Zwift for a lot of people. Wahoo is far and away the market leader when it comes to indoor trainers but the brand has a bit of a challenge on it’s hands. The offerings have gotten so good over the years that it’s hard to recommend the more expensive options. Adding the Cog and Click makes it even easier to add your outdoor bike. I have this as the best smart trainer for Zwift in my best smart trainers buyers guide and that means the best overall in my mind. Grab a great deal now before winter really hits.

One of the keys to eating enough on long rides is mixing textures and flavors. I generally drink my calories when riding, but I always carry chews so I can stop briefly and chew something.

Like I said, I tend to prefer to drink my calories on the bike, and this is my go-to choice. There’s a decent amount of sodium and a sweet, but not sickly, flavor profile. You can also choose an option with caffeine if that is your preference.

There’s science behind the idea that cramps come from a hyper-excited motor neuron repeatedly misfiring and locking the muscle up, rather than just dehydration or an electrolyte imbalance, and that it’s possible to make it stop with a shock to the vagus nerve. That shock comes from sour foods, so I also carry sour Salt Stick Energy Gummies with me. To be clear, Salt Stick doesn’t make this claim, and its gummies might not be sour enough. I don’t worry too much though because they still taste delicious and the cramp relief is just a potential bonus. You also get 130 mg of salt per packet, so that helps with cramps too.

If you aren’t in the Apple ecosystem, then I find the choice for headphones that are perfect for on and off the bike to be a lot more wide open. I’ve gone back and forth with different companies who offer a little more this or that, but in the end, I keep coming back to the Pixel Buds Pro 2 because the mic is really good and there’s such easy access to Gemini. For Android users who want headphones that will work just as well off the bike as on, this is my choice.

If you enjoy the videos that I put out for Velo, this is one of the two cameras that I use. Insta360 has a huge range of fantastic products, but I’ve settled into the GO Ultra as my second camera, which I attach to my jersey for a second point of view. It’s also a fantastic choice for regular life as you can use it as a tiny still/video travel camera when it’s docked. You can read my full Insta360 GO Ultra review for more info.

The other camera I use to make videos is the Mission 1 Pro. As good as Insta360 and DJI are, nothing else currently competes with the quality of the Mission 1 Pro. This is a professional-level tool for anyone serious about the best quality content. You can read more in my full GoPro Mission 1 Pro review .

One of the best things about Garmin is the way that the ecosystem lets you move between devices seamlessly. I don’t have to wear a strap or a watch while I ride because I have a Garmin bike computer (not on sale for Prime Day). When I get off the bike and put on the watch, the data seamlessly switches so that’s all uninterrupted in Garmin Connect. That opens up a small need for something different in my watch, though. I want something that looks good and works as a smartwatch as much as a fitness watch. That’s where the Garmin Venu X1 fits in.…

items.title: Ezra Caudell Leaves the Hospital 31 Days After Philadelphia Crash
items.author: ahood
items.content: Modern Adventure rider Ezra Caudell will begin intensive rehabilitation as his recovery from the Philadelphia crash progresses, officials confirmed Tuesday.
items.lbText:
Ezra Caudell, shown here this spring, has left a hospital after a month following his crash. (Photo: Gautier Demouveaux/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Ezra Caudell has left the hospital and is transferring into intensive rehabilitation some 31 days after his traumatic crash at the Philadelphia Cycling Classic .

The Modern Adventure Pro Cycling rider was discharged late last week and will continue his recovery at Magee Rehabilitation Hospital in Philadelphia, officials confirmed.

Caudell, 20, was already walking the hospital halls before his discharge , according to the recovery update shared by his family and team.

“Just as encouraging has been his neurologic recovery. Ezra continues to show significant improvement from the injury to his brain, with progress in his strength, cognition, communication, and independence each day,” an update read.

“His recovery will take time, but his progress over the past month has been remarkable, and to see him now walking, interacting with those around him, and moving on to rehabilitation represents an enormous milestone.”

Caudell crashed on August 30 while racing the Philadelphia Cycling Classic.

The move into rehabilitation marks a major step for Caudell, though the team update on Tuesday emphasized that a long recovery still lies ahead.

The medical team expects his lung contusions and his fractures to continue healing without the need for further intervention, officials said.

His family and Modern Adventure Pro Cycling thanked supporters for their continued support as the popular rider begins the next phase of recovery.

“Ezra’s family and the Modern Adventure Pro Cycling team have every confidence in him and remain deeply grateful for the continued support he has received,” a note read.

items.title: Fractured Neck, Broken Collarbone, Relegation: Coppa Bernocchi Crash Takes Heavy Toll
items.author: ahood
items.content: Raccagni could face surgery, Aranburu’s season is over, and Van den Berg loses third after a chaotic, crash-marred final 600 meters at Coppa Bernocchi. And that's not counting a delivery van that drove onto the course.
items.lbText:
Ben Swift, inset, finished with cuts and gashes after a big crash at the end of Coppa Bernocchi. (Photo: Getty Images)

Andrea Raccagni fractured a neck vertebra and Alex Aranburu broke his collarbone and part of his pelvis in a brutal, high-speed crash Monday at the Coppa Bernocchi .

Marijn van den Berg (EF Education-EasyPost) lost his podium place after the race jury relegated him in a messy finale to the Italian classic.

The pileup tore through the bunch about 600 meters from the finish in Legnano as riders were fighting for position ahead of a reduced bunch sprint.

Netcompany-Ineos riders Ben Swift and Filippo Ganna were among those gong down in the crash, and one rider smashed heavily into an unpadded light post.

Swift — who is retiring this season — crossed the line with cuts and gashes, but is still hoping to race Paris-Tours later this month.

Raccagni suffered a fracture of his third cervical vertebra, Soudal Quick-Step confirmed after hospital examinations that included a CT scan. The Italian was scheduled for assessment by surgeons Tuesday.

“He will be assessed by surgeons tomorrow to determine the most appropriate course of treatment and recovery,” the team said in its Monday statement.

Aranburu sustained fractures to his right collarbone and iliac wing, a part of the pelvis, Cofidis announced.

The race jury relegated Van den Berg, who crossed the line third, to 33rd to last in the finishing group after a wild race in the mid-week classic.

Race footage showed the EF Education-EasyPost rider making shoulder contact with eventual winner Noa Isidore (Decathlon-CMA CGM) while moving up on wide roads.

Isidore swerved and made contact with Swift, who fell at speed and brought down several riders behind him. Riders fell into a cement curb and one rider struck a light post at high speed.

Isidore stayed upright and won the ensuing sprint ahead of Tommaso Dati (Team UKYO). Van den Berg’s relegation moved Movistar’s Orluis Aular into third.

items.title: The Kenda Velora Tire Review: Modern Endurance Road
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The new premium road offering from Kenda brings a lot more puncture protection and improved speed to its endurance platform.
items.lbText:
Kenda has launched the Velora Endurance, a new set of endurance road tires that offer a premium feel with a range of puncture-resistant long-haul options.

The Velora brings durability and low rolling resistance to the table, with Kenda claiming major improvements in puncture protection and watts saved over its previous models. The model also comes in three sizes: 28, 32, and 35 mm.

With Kenda’s re-entry into the premium endurance tire market—in addition to other tires like the Silca Protocol RCR —the 32-40 mm range for all-road tires is quickly filling out. Not too long ago, that range of tires was a quirky grey area between road and gravel, but now it serves as another area of the industry where there are scores of good options.

Read on to see how the Kenda Velora Endurance fits into the mix. Hint: it’s one of the better options available.

While the Velora Endurance brings new options to the endurance/all-road tire market, Kenda is taking a fairly traditional approach overall with this model. It’s built, first and foremost, for durability.

That durability is derived primarily from the puncture-resistant base layer of the tire casing. Instead of loading puncture-resistance features into the entire tread, the base layer runs just along the center of the tread. This keeps the tire weight low and the tire relatively thin, despite the 35 percent improvement in the center tread’s ability to withstand debris and detritus.

While the Velora prioritizes the same puncture resistance as previous endurance tires, it is still a big evolution from the heavy, plodding endurance tires of years past. Kenda pairs the endurance-oriented puncture-resistant base layer with a premium rubber compound that is much more pitched towards speed.

To find this speed, the Velora uses the new K-Series rubber compound that has been slowly rolled out across several of Kenda’s recent new releases. That new rubber compound has been specifically formulated for performance on tarmac and yields a significant 12-watt reduction in rolling resistance compared to the previous Kenda endurance tire.

While Kenda also claims better rolling resistance compared to unnamed competitors, there is no third-party data yet for the tire’s overall rolling efficiency.

That being said, that compound is built to be both fast and durable. Kenda claims that the Velora Endurance is very wear-resistant, with a 27 percent reduction in tread degradation compared to the brand’s previous endurance tires. You could say the Velora is built for endurance in more ways than just long rides.

Lastly, while the tire is firmly a road tire, it does have prominent shoulder “siping” that runs in clusters along the tire. Those sipes, which are thin grooves cut into the shoulder of the tire, are specifically designed to help boost traction in wet environments. The grooves help funnel water away from the broad, slick center tread, which boosts traction especially on slick corners. The siping also helps add a bit of traction in dry conditions when riding on light, loose-over-hard conditions.

Over the last month, I have been able to put a few hundred miles on the 32 and 35mm versions of the Velora Endurance tires, and I have been very pleased with how the tires feel and perform in the right circumstances.

Personally, I felt more of a draw to the 35mm option as there are just fewer great options at that width. Additionally, as tires have gotten bigger, 30-32 mm is the range of width I use for race tires, so testing the 32mm—let alone the 28mm—just didn’t feel like it made much sense. Instead, having a nice 35mm endurance tire was the perfect pair for some adventures on the new Trek Domane, a modern endurance bike with clearance up to 40mm.

Would I have loved to try the Velora in 38-40 mm? Absolutely, but unfortunately, Kenda cut things off at 35mm. Nevertheless, I found the 35s had a great balance of versatility, reliability, and speed that really surprised me.

Out of the box, the Velora Endurance tires do look and feel like endurance tires. They have more structure, they feel on the heavier side, and the center tread is notably a bit thicker and more rigid than a pure road racing tire. But even with those attributes, the sidewalls felt fairly flexible. When I was mounting it onto the rim, the tire also felt more similar to a good racing tire than a rigid, heavier endurance tire.

Speaking of weight, the Velora is certainly no featherweight, but it holds its own. At 370g for the 35mm, the tire is about middle of the pack—similar to the Specialized Mondo, lighter than the Pirelli P-Zero, and heavier than the Silca RCR.

After the installation, I found that the tire felt alive straight away. There wasn’t any of the stiffness you might get from a tire with thick, new rubber. Instead, it rolled pretty fast and handled well, with the tire holding its structure even at a relatively low 50 PSI of pressure. One of my nitpicks with mid-width slicks is how inconsistent they can feel. The heavier, thicker tires can be too rigid and can be harsh and bouncy, neither of which inspires much confidence during cornering or at speed. Others are too light, and those can feel muddled and squishy at “all-road” pressure—even worse for confidence.

The Velora Endurance has a good balance between rigidity and suppleness. My guess is that comes from the tire’s split personality, with a fast rubber compound and strong-but-narrow puncture protection creating an effective pairing for that balanced handling.

The out-and-out speed of the tire is where things are less clear. The big test for the tire’s speed was a long Saturday group ride that functions a bit like a segmented race. The first two efforts are both uphill drags, a perfect scenario to feel a tire’s overall speed, before I would set off on my own up a gravel road and a long, steep gravel climb to test the all-road chops of the tire.…

items.title: Giulio Ciccone Questions European Championships Photo Finish Against Remco Evenepoel
items.author: ahood
items.content: ‘I’ve watched the available footage hundreds of times’: The Italian wants to see the decisive image after missing European gold by 0.0028 seconds.
items.lbText:
Ciccone reacts after losing the European Championships in a photo finish. (Photo: Getty Images)

Giulio Ciccone wants to see the image that decided the European road title for himself, because he still has doubts about Sunday’s razor-thin defeat .

The Italian said he still cannot come to terms with the photo finish verdict and footage of his dramatic loss against Remco Evenepoel .

“The title was awarded by a margin of 0.0028 seconds, or 2.8 thousandths of a second,” Ciccone wrote on Instagram.

“I’ve watched the available footage hundreds of times and, in the shots where the finish line is visible, I keep seeing something that I cannot reconcile with that verdict.”

Evenepoel snagged gold Sunday with a spectacular bike throw in Slovenia to edge out the Italian in a two-up sprint so tight that it took a photo finish to call the winner.

On Monday, Ciccone praised the Belgian’s performance and defended his racing tactics, but said he wanted to see the evidence for himself.

“Remco was the strongest rider yesterday,” he wrote. “I’m asking for something very simple: to see the photo finish at the actual finish line.”

Ciccone said commissaires and federation technical staff explained Monday morning how the photo finish works and the criteria used to interpret it.

But that’s not enough for the 31-year-old Lidl-Trek star to accept the outcome.

“So I’m not asking for another explanation,” he wrote. “I’m asking to see the photo finish that corresponds exactly to the actual finish line.”

Ciccone’s questions followed a brutally close finish to Sunday’s wild and wide-open European Championship.

Ciccone and Evenepoel dueled to the end, with the Italian looking to have the winning edge after out-positioning the Belgian on the final corner. Evenepoel opened up a desperate burst in the closing meters and timed his bike throw perfectly at the line.

After a long and tense wait, the race jury eventually awarded the victory to Evenepoel.

In a lengthy public post on Monday, the Italian said he wants to see the photo of both wheels crossing the line.

“Because if a European title is decided by 2.8 thousandths of a second, I believe it is legitimate to ask for that crossing to be shown with the same precision used to determine the result,” he wrote.

“If that image confirms the verdict, there will be nothing more to add,” he wrote. “But until I’m shown that correspondence, a question remains for me that has yet to be answered.”

On Monday evening, the Union Européenne de Cyclisme — which runs and organizes the European championships — issued the following statement:

“The Union Européenne de Cyclisme (UEC) informs that the photo-finish system used at the 2026 UEC Road European Championships (EtherLynx Vision PRO X) records the finish line thousands of times per second (13,000 in the specific case of the European Championship races), making it possible to determine the finishing order with extreme precision, even when the differences are minimal,” a media note read.

“It is important to clarify that a photo finish is not a traditional photograph. The final image is composed of the chronological sequence of recordings made at the finish line; for this reason, the horizontal axis represents time, not distance. This can create apparent distortions of wheels, bicycles and riders, without any impact on the accuracy of the result.

“In cycling, the determining reference is the most advanced part (tangent) of the front wheel at the moment it reaches the finish line. At the European Championships, two independent photo-finish systems were used, providing two separate images to verify the result.”

items.title: Silca Protocol RCR 29 Review: Go Bigger
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Silca built a 29mm tire with great ride feel, but that fails to stand out in any strong way. If you want to beat the competition, you have to look at a different size.
items.lbText:
Comfortable ride feel Excellent dry cornering grip High puncture resistance for a race tire Competitive weight-to-width ratio Aerodynamically optimized width Excellent choice in 38mm size

Silca recently launched a new series of tires. The lineup covers both road and gravel, and everything offered is focused on high volume and ride feel. Of course, they launched without much of a bang, and there definitely weren’t any major claims made… No, I am obviously kidding. This is Silca, and these tires launched to so much hype it hurt. The claim was that they were head and shoulders above the rest of the field.

Then Bicycle Rolling Resistance put the RCR 29 through its testing regime, and the results were… a bit lackluster. Big claims have now been made on the other side of the fence, but not that many people have actually ridden these tires. I’ve now got a few hundred miles on them, and I think there’s more to these tires than a drum test—but I don’t love everything. Let’s look at the good and the bad when it comes to the Silca RCR 29 road tires.

What I do on a bike—almost always a race bike—is ride it longer than anyone expects. I want a tire that soaks up rough pavement, but I’m not running 34mm tires because I also want aerodynamics in a straight line, and I’m not interested in increasing wheel width (meaning weight) to optimize for a wider tire. In other words, I want to have my cake and eat it too.

I’ve been running the Silca 29mm tires at 52 psi on a 22.5mm internal width rim, and to me, they pull this balance off. A 29mm width matches well with modern rims in terms of the Rule of 105 and aerodynamics. That 29mm also means if you are a stickler for following ETRTO recommendations, you can run a 25mm internal width rim, but that’s not something I worry about.

Where I find the Silca tires really shining is cornering in the dry. Bicycle Rolling Resistance doesn’t test dry cornering because it’s universally quite high, but these tires have tested high in wet grip. Personally, I don’t care a ton about wet grip because these are on a bike that won’t see much rain, but I do think there’s nuance in dry pavement cornering grip, and these land in my “good bucket.”

Lean the bike, stand on the outside pedal, and you can feel the bite. Over and over, I surprised myself by cutting tight switchbacks a little tighter than I normally would, while still feeling confident and in control. A big part of this feeling goes back to a tire that does a great job soaking up bumps. Even on a stiff race bike, I don’t find the front wheel coming off the line over small cracks.

That means the real advantage again goes back to that ride feel, but sometimes that is accompanied by the puncture protection of an overinflated water balloon. That’s not the case here. Even before the BRR testing, I had a guess that it was decent based on the 2.1mm tread thickness. That matches the GP5000 thickness, and while thickness isn’t an exact 1:1 for puncture protection, it’s a decent way of setting expectations. BRR confirmed exactly what I expected, although it is a bit lower than the P Zero Race RS (which is also thicker). My own experience here is that all of the popular race tires are pretty close in puncture protection, and it’s good enough. Silca falls in line.

Basically, the Silca tire falls into the “good enough” bucket. I told you it has good ride feel, cornering grip, and puncture protection, and that should be enough, right? It is enough, but why are you choosing the Silca tire?

The Continental GP5000, Schwalbe Pro One, Pirelli P Zero Race RS, Goodyear Eagle F1 R Z29 Aero, and Vittoria Corsa Pro are all good tires with slight advantages and disadvantages. Maybe one leans a little this way and another a little that way, but it’s incredibly close. I doubt I can convince dedicated Vittoria fans to switch to the Zipp/Goodyear tire, and equally, for what reason would you switch from your favorite tire to the Silca? What is the unique selling proposition for Silca?

Given that Silca is all about marginal gains, I really wanted to see these come out as an aero-optimized tire. I’ve talked to Josh Poertner about aero tires plenty this year, and I know he believes in them, but the RCR is not an aero tire. When I asked for clarification, the answer was that, at this point, he doesn’t have a way to add aero gains without losing rolling resistance.

It’s a fair answer and it makes a lot of sense, but it would also make you think the Silca tires excel at rolling resistance. Now that Bicycle Rolling Resistance has tested that they are mid-pack, that’s a tough argument to make, too. Silca claims that the RCR is faster than the Vittoria Corsa Pro Control, and BRR confirmed that it’s 3.6 watts faster at 72 psi. That’s a win, but the same testing shows the GP5000 as 1.8 watts faster than the RCR.

I won’t argue that 1.8 watts is worth choosing the GP5000, but is anyone going to argue that the GP5000 is a tire that lacks cornering grip or that the ride feel isn’t good? I might even say the Silca tire has better ride feel, but it’s about as subtle as 1.8 watts. It’s worth noting that Silca also has better puncture protection, but I’m still not convinced any of this is quite enough to get people jumping brands.

The main negative I see here is the lack of a compelling reason for people to switch brands. The Silca RCR 29 is another good tire, but it’s not doing anything special. I, for one, can’t wait for Poertner to crack the aero nut without harming puncture protection or rolling resistance.

This could be the place where the Silca RCR tires gain some converts. The product description has a section that covers “Carbon BeadLock technology,” which is a technology Silca is using to swap the normal Kevlar bead “with non-stretching carbon fiber to eliminate moisture absorption, stretch, and tire wobble for a precise rim fit over the entire lifespan of the tire.”…

items.title: ‘Speak With Data’: UAE Boss Slams Skeptics Fueling Del Toro-McNulty Conspiracy Theories
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: McNulty and Del Toro's trade team manager defends Mexican amid talk of illegal collusion with USA at world championships: 'He was strongest, even if McNulty won.'
items.lbText:
Did Isaac del Toro help his UAE trade teammate Brandon McNulty win the road world title?

That’s the debate that’s doing the rounds after McNulty brought the U.S. its first rainbow jersey in 33 years at the UCI road world championships last weekend.

“Del Toro was obviously working for McNulty,” gnashed Tom Pidcock in the aftermath of a wild race in Montréal.

Michael Matthews insinuated similar as Team USA’s losing rivals picked apart what went wrong last Sunday.

The Tin Foil Hat Brigade has been picking over race replays and sparking conspiracy theories ever since.

Was there a nefarious trade team alliance in this race of nations?

Speaking to QuiBici Sport , McNulty and Del Toro’s manager at UAE Emirates-XRG dismissed the doubters.

If the Mexican Del Toro somehow colluded with Team USA after McNulty slipped away with his decisive attack, Joxean Fernández Matxin wants to see proof.

“To anyone who insinuates this, I urge you to speak with data and not with opinions,” Matxin told Qui Bici Sport . “How long was Del Toro on the front? And the others who are talking, how long were they on the front trying to close it down?

“If you bring me evidence with numbers showing that he pulled less than the others, then I can agree with you,” Matxin said. “But if they are just words, with all due respect, it remains an opinion we can all form.”

Matxin’s words of defense are hardly a surprise.

He’s in the upper tier of management at UAE, the super team boasting Del Toro, McNulty, and Tadej Pogačar on the books and now a third straight year hosting the reigning world champion.

Of course he’ll say McNulty won fair and square.

But even without any possible supporting data, the evidence was all over the TV screens.

Del Toro was the most active rider in the race, despite representing one of cycling’s minnow nations.

“He wanted to win worlds,” Matxin said. “He defends the colors of Mexico because he is proud to be Mexican. He wants to make history for his country.”

Matxin went as far as to say that his Tour de France podium-finisher was the best rider in Montréal.

“In my opinion, Del Toro was the strongest, even if Brandon won. You could see that in how the other riders marked him,” Matxin told QuiBici . “The course may not have been the best for him, but in terms of condition, he was superior to everyone.”

With Pogačar on the sidelines and Remco Evenepoel on an off-day, it was a rainbow opportunity Del Toro would never throw away.

Speaking to Velo last week, Team USA sport director Mike Creed and cult favorite road captain Larry Warbasse also dismissed the collusion conspiracy .

The theory that Del Toro switched passports in the final of road worlds was, according to Warbasse, “ridiculous.”

“You don’t pull all day and then just give the race to McNulty,” Creed told Velo . “If you just finished 270km and you’re frustrated, and your name is Tom Pidcock, that’s understandable.

“For everyone else, it’s just stirring the pot,” Creed continued. “I don’t know anyone who would give away the world championships.”

So why didn’t Del Toro pull the chasers when McNulty launched his winning raid?

One, he was probably gassed. He’d just been riding the front for the best part of 40km.

Two, he was isolated and caught at the opposite end of the spectrum from USA, who flooded the zone with McNulty, Matteo Jorgenson, and Quinn Simmons.

Del Toro wasn’t shy when he debriefed the race to ESPN MX last week.

His rivals exploited Mexico’s collective weakness, and he couldn’t do more when his race started to unravel.

“The peloton raced a little against us or used the fact we didn’t have the best team,” Del Toro told ESPN MX .

“I didn’t want the gold medal to get away from me,” he added. “Finally, though, it was very difficult for me to keep going, and I ran fifth, unfortunately. It’s a bittersweet taste.”

If Team USA paid Del Toro for his role in McNulty’s world title, the Mexican clearly invested in some good acting classes.

Speculation aside, McNulty now owns the rainbow jersey for the next 12 months.

Despite the background debate, the consensus is that the 28-year-old earned the stripes courtesy of individual strength and the smarts of U.S. nationals.

McNulty hasn’t publicly spoken out about the Del Toro drama, and it’s hard to imagine he ever will.

However, the shy Arizonan could barely hide his delight after he debuted his new striped top this weekend in Italy.

McNulty hit 10th at the Giro dell’Emila on Saturday and narrowly missed the win Sunday at Coppa Agostoni.

“For sure it is still settling in, with the jersey and everything,” McNulty said Sunday after he finished second in the six-rider sprint.

“It is super special [being the world champion],” McNulty said Sunday. “I feel like the races pass faster; I don’t really think about kilometers to go anymore. Hopefully that continues. Perhaps it will wear off, and I will go back to suffering, but the last two days have been so special.”

McNulty gets two more shots at winning in rainbows before he shuts down his 2026 season.

The hilly circuits of Tre Valle Varesine await on Wednesday.

Three days later, McNulty teams up at UAE Emirates-XRG with – guess who – Del Toro for a monument brawl with Evenepoel and Paul Seixas at Il Lombardia.

That’s a race where the American and Mexican will race together.

items.title: What’s Brandon McNulty’s Road Worlds Title Worth? Not Much, and a Lot
items.author: ahood
items.content: Analysis: Brandon McNulty earned €8,000 for his road world title. What could bonuses, contracts, and sponsors add to his payday?
items.lbText:
McNulty celebrates the world title in Montréal and it remains to be seen how much economic windfall it will deliver. (Photo: Filip Bezdek/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Brandon McNulty ended America’s 33-year drought for a men’s UCI road world title in Montréal, beat a field stacked with cycling’s biggest stars, and earned himself a rainbow jersey.

But the prize money alone won’t make him rich.

That’s the official paycheck for winning one of the sport’s most coveted races. Michael Matthews earned €4,000 for silver, Mathieu van der Poel collected €2,000 for bronze, and everyone else earned no official prize money.

Of course, McNulty was chasing a place in cycling history, not a down payment on a yacht, when he won America’s first elite men’s road title since Lance Armstrong in 1993 .

But what are those stripes really worth?

The prize money is the same for men and women in Montréal, but things get potentially more lucrative once agents, team bonuses, sponsorship deals, and long-term contracts enter the calculation.

First off, professional riders earn their paycheck from their respective trade teams, not from chasing the rainbow bands.

Racing the worlds with national teams is a unique, one-off event each season where money isn’t the primary motivation. It’s for the love of the game.

In fact, racing for the national team rarely earns the riders any extra dosh at all.

USA Cycling does not pay its road riders an appearance fee to compete at the world championships . The U.S. federation — which receives no government funding — covers travel, accommodation, meals, and the support staff behind the race.

The federation also provides coaches, mechanics, soigneurs , and the other staff needed to keep the national squad rolling.

That’s pretty much the same across the entire peloton.

Some riders used to be paid to race worlds when federation budgets were healthier, especially in cycling’s European heartland. Today, most national teams only cover expenses without paying riders simply to take the start.

So even big stars like Van der Poel or newly crowned world champion Demi Vollering do not receive race money from the Dutch federation simply for showing up.

Some riders even had to buy their own plane ticket to Montréal.

New Zealand’s top pro riders had to cover their costs to race in Montréal, and many junior and U23 ranks across many nations had to as well.

Mads Pedersen deserves kudos when he auctioned off some racing memorabilia and contributed funding to help a pair of U23 riders join the Danish squad in Canada.

Magdeleine Vallières paid for her flight to Rwanda and supplementary team fees before winning the women’s road race in Kigali last year.

The payoff was huge after she won Canada’s first elite road world title.

At least she was closer to home in Montréal last month.

Cycling isn’t known for its huge winners’ paychecks anyway , but the worlds is small by any measure.

Despite the world crown being one of cycling’s most prestigious titles, at €8,000, it almost looks like someone forgot to add a zero.

That’s even less than what an individual stage winner receives in the men’s Tour de France at €11,000 , or the winner of the men’s Tour of Flanders at €20,000.

Winning the rainbow jersey might not earn much on race day, but it pays off in many other ways.

Most top pros will have performance bonuses written into their trade-team contracts. One agent told Velo that performance bonuses are packed in for big wins at races like the monuments and the world championships.

The amounts depend on the rider, the team, and what everyone agreed around the negotiating table. Tadej Pogačar, for example, receives €250,000 for winning the stripes from his trade team contract .

The champion wears the rainbow jersey in road races until the next world championships, giving teams such as UAE Emirates-XRG and FDJ United-Suez plenty of publicity and exposure for their sponsors.

Whether McNulty or Vollering received a worlds bonus, and how much, remains private.

A big win like the world title could produce a big “worlds bounce” in terms of salary negotiating power for the right kind of rider.

In McNulty’s case, that’s hard to say because he already settled his long-term future in April when he extended his UAE contract through the end of 2030.

That does not prevent the two sides from renegotiating the deal — like Pogačar recently did with his contract extension through 2032 — but winning in Montréal does not automatically change an existing salary agreement.

When McNulty and UAE signed that deal this spring , it was months before he won the rainbow jersey. Hopefully, a smart agent at least included a winner’s bonus.

One agent told Velo that today’s market places a premium on youth and future potential.

A world crown strengthens McNulty’s palmarès , but it might not bring a huge salary bump, especially with his future already locked in.

Then there is the question of what McNulty might earn beyond his team contract.

Everyone knows pro bike racing is hardly front-page news in the U.S.

In fact, McNulty said he gave only one pre-race interview before his victory, and that was to Belgian broadcaster Sporza .

His victory drew coverage from The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal , both of which cover cycling regularly.

Whether his win translates into wider American exposure remains to be seen, but it’s unlikely he’ll be on a Wheaties box anytime soon.

He might land sponsorship opportunities within cycling and earn appearance fees at critériums and promotional events . There could also be opportunities closer to home in Arizona.

Of course, not everything is about money.

What’s certain is that McNulty will wear the rainbow jersey until the next world championships and the champion’s bands for the rest of his career.

Those stripes put McNulty in rare company, one of just five Americans to win an elite road race world title .

items.title: Formula 1 Superstar Valtteri Bottas Is Cycling From Malaysia to Singapore for His Next Grand Prix
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Some drivers would take a private jet for the long journey from Sepang to Singapore – but not Bottas, the F1 racer-turned gravel aficionado.
items.lbText:
Valtteri Bottas is decompressing from a disappointing DNF at Sunday’s Grand Prix in Malaysia by cycling some 350km to his next race.

It’s not the usual way Formula 1 drivers choose to recover from the mind-zapping fatigue and furnace-like conditions of a 300kph race in stormy Southeast Asia.

But it’s the way that F1’s elite gravel cycling convert has decided will work for him.

On Sunday night, Bottas completed “Leg 1” of a multi-day adventure ride toward this coming weekend’s Singapore Grand Prix.

The 37-year-old Cadillac driver had spun out on lap nine of a wet and wild race on the Sepang International Circuit on Sunday, which was being used as a substitute venue for the originally planned race in Bahrain.

Not long after stripping out of his overalls, Bottas clocked 56km in little more than two hours of night-time riding heading southeast toward Si Rusa.

The veteran car driver and Canyon bikes ambassador posted a video to Instagram showing him bumping his way across gravelly trails, followed by a #foodporn photo of a boutique dinner upon arrival in the popular tourist spot on the Malaysian coast.

With a base salary of around $5 million USD, Bottas hardly needs to “dirtbag” his journey, after all.

Bottas is famed for his off-the-racetrack exploits.

He’s been riding bikes for years and more recently integrated into the gravel racing scene through his partner, Tiffany Cromwell. He’s scored podium finishes at SBT Gravel and the Belgium Waffle Ride, and helped establish the FNLD GRVL event.

Bottas told his sponsors at Canyon earlier this year that he sees the bike as good for both his body and his mind.

“When I’m on my bike, I gain cardio, but I also use the bike almost like a stress release, you know? In a way, it’s a great way to clear my head if I have a bit of stress, and a chance to explore,” he said.

“It’s also a way for me to challenge myself when I’m not racing in my car. And when I miss racing, then I race on my bicycle.”

And while Bottas hasn’t spoken publicly about his trans-Grands Prix adventure this week, he must see it as a timely pressure release.

The long-time bike lover qualified for the UCI Gravel World Championships in Australia on October 11 after he finished fifth in his age group at the gravel world series event in Hlinsko, Czech Republic.

However, the champs had to go on ice for Bottas.

They clash directly with the approaching Singapore GP, where he and his Cadillac teammate Sergio Pérez will chase some much-needed points to claw their way out of the bottom of the F1 drivers’ championship.

items.title: ‘He Felt Really Guilty’: Worlds Defeat Had Bigger Impact than Believed on Evenepoel
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Remco Evenepoel grabs victory in Euro road championships by the tiniest margin, then renounces TT defense.
items.lbText:
Remco Evenepoel (r) celebrates winning the European road race championship in Ljubljana, Slovenia (Photo: David Pintens / Belga Mag via AFP) (Photo: DAVID PINTENS)

The huge roar Remco Evenepoel let out when the photo finish result was confirmed said it all: winning the European road race championship was a massive release.

Second in the Tour de France, first in the GP Cycliste de Quebec and first in the world TT championships saw Evenepoel line out in the worlds road race as a big favorite. That hope unraveled with a curiously subdued performance and a distant 12th place.

Missing out on the win hurt, but so too letting down the national team and the Belgian supporters. He was billed beforehand as one of the main contenders and his compatriots worked very hard to put him in the position to win.

Not delivering on that was hard to take but, until Sunday, it was something he had played down.

“It was honestly a really tough week for me after the deception [disappointment] of the worlds,” Evenepoel said shortly after being confirmed as the new European champion. “It was playing more in my head than I have been showing, so it is a big relief to be back on a good level today and to complete my championship jerseys. It feels amazing.”

Indeed, the 26-year-old looked to have the weight of the world lift off his mind, something his wife Oumi confirmed.

“He likes to pretend to be tougher than he is, but he felt very guilty towards his teammates, the federation and the Belgian fans,” she told VTM News on Sunday afternoon.

“I’m extra happy that he can take home that jersey, the only one he missed.”

Evenepoel didn’t have it easy in the race. The Belgian team did incredible work to set things up for him and paved the way for a huge attack the penultimate time up the climb.

He blasted clear with Giulio Ciccone for company, but then hit the deck on a tight uphill curve.

“I went a bit too fast in the corner and I just slipped away,” he said Sunday afternoon, referring to his front wheel. “I think there I could have gone, but in the end we stayed calm and we came back to the plan. Then I put in an attack just before the descent and then I was with Cicco in the front.”

Getting back to Ciccone was crucial but, in the end, the Italian did very little of the work. He had learned his teammate Christian Scaroni was chasing alone and that meant he further pulled back on any collaboration. However he did finally do a turn close to the finish after both the Belgian and the Italian team cars pulled alongside to advise their riders.

There were no race radios allowed and so speaking directly to the team managers had extra importance.

Belgian team chief Serge Pauwels did communicate Evenepoel; what did he say to him?

“That the gap with Scaroni was 50 seconds, that he should try and back off a little bit in the last kilometer, that it was safe to do the sprint,” he answered. “Because we knew of course that Ciccone wasn’t working any more.

“I hoped that even if it worked a little bit then it was maybe enough, because the difference in the end wasn’t that big.”

That’s certainly the case: Ciccone rounded the final bend in a much better way and got the jump on his rival, with Evenepoel approximately three lengths back and chasing desperately.

He closed and closed, and won the race with a much better lunge for the line. The difference?

According to HLN , it was just .00028 of a second.

The official result came through soon afterward and the explosion of sound from Evenepoel and his team showed what it meant.

“Honestly, I felt I was really coming over him,” said Evenepoel. “I thought that I was going to win it, but you never know. I think the images were really clear, the big relief that I felt and how proud I am to take the victory today.

“Like I said, it was a really tough week mentally to recover from the deception and to put a deception for my country on the world championships. I hope that I made everyone proud today.”

He did, but his fans are going to have to make do with the road race as his sole European title this time around. He had never won that particular contest, other than as a junior, but he does have two past Euro TT titles to his credit.

A third would be almost guaranteed if he competed, given his form in winning the world championship TT.

Evenepoel is fast approaching the end of his season. He’s never won Il Lombardia , with big rival Tadej Pogačar taking the past five editions. He was however second in 2024 and 2025 and, with Pogačar absent due to injury, will fancy his chances.

Because of that, he has taken the big decision to give up the chance of winning another TT title.

“No, no, I am going to focus on Lombardia now,” he said, when asked if he’d be lining out in the time trial on Wednesday.

It’s a brave and somewhat risky decision to make but taking the road race title for the first time has given him the result he was really chasing.

It’s also a huge reassurance following his dejection in the Canadian worlds.

“I am going to celebrate tonight because it is a special one,” he smiled.

“Like I said, now I won all the championships in pro cycling, so I think this one we can celebrate big time.”

It is, and even more so after last weekend didn’t go to plan.

“I’m happy for him, because otherwise I had to comfort him again,” his wife said, smiling.

items.title: ‘My Shape Is Really Bad’: Tadej Pogačar Sorry/Not Sorry to Miss Euro Champs
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Speculation growing about when and where Pogačar could return to racing in 2027. His team and others comment.
items.lbText:
Tadej Pogačar and his partner Urska Žigart attend the elite men's European road race championships as spectators (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski/Getty Images) (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski)

There was much chatter recently that Tadej Pogačar might defy team orders and ride the European championships , both to defend his title and also because it was held in his home country of Slovenia.

His team denied it and said his recovery was too important, and so it proved: the 28 year old was at the race, but only as a guest.

Winning a major title on home soil is likely a once in a lifetime possibility for a Slovenian but, in this case at least, it’s one ambition he may have to let go of.

Ditto for his partner Urška Žigart, who is also sidelined after a jawbone fracture reoccurred again.

“For sure even yesterday when we were watching the women’s race, Urška was like, ‘damn, I should be there,” Pogačar told Eurosport after the finish of Sunday’s race.

“Especially she has been feeling super good so it is tough. When you have good shape it is tough to look at the race and know you could be part of it.”

Pogačar has been in dominant form this year, winning a record-equaling fifth Tour de France plus multiple other races. He looked to be en route for victory at the Vuelta a España but crashed heavily on stage 8 and withdrew.

He was diagnosed with a fractured vertebra and collarbone, as well as concussion. And while he’s recovered rapidly from that fall, he’s also realistic about how he would have got on had he defied his team and ridden on Sunday.

“Today I am riding my bike for one week now outside. I know my shape is really bad,” he said. “I don’t wish to be riding out today. But one week ago or two weeks ago, I would be really eager to be on the start today.”

The question of when Pogačar will be on a startline again still remains to be seen.

El Pais recently suggested he would contradict UAE Team Emirates-XRG advice and line out in the European championships, something the team denied.

And while he ultimately didn’t take part in the race, the Spanish publication stated that competing in the Santos Tour Down Under would be the team’s preferred first race back.

That’s something we at Velo previously argued , noting that both the rider himself and Pogačar’s own agent Alex Carera had said earlier this season that the Slovenian was planning to ride—and win—the race at some point in the coming years.

He has made winning every WorldTour stage race a big career goal and the early finish to his racing in 2026 seems to tee things up perfectly for an early season start.

Such a buildup could also put him in prime form for Paris-Roubaix, a race he has been trying to win.

Velo reached out in recent weeks to the race organisers, to Carera and to UAE Team Emirates-XRG.

His agent didn’t reply as yet, but Santos Tour Down Under organisers were non-committal about the prospect of him competing there.

“Our only thought right now, like every cycling fan in the world, is for Tadej and Urska in their recovery from their injuries,” a spokesperson told Velo in late August. “We hope to see them back on their bike soon and wish them all the best, but anything beyond that is secondary to their health and wellbeing.”

A spokesperson in recent days said it was far too early to get confirmation of his plans, noting that the first indications of his schedule would be given out at the team’s December camp.

He may well decide to head to Australia, a race he previously rode in 2019. But it seems confirmation of that is still a couple of months away.

For now, watching races and rebuilding his fitness will be as close as he will get to pinning on a number.

items.title: Evenepoel Pips Ciccone in Desperate Sprint to Become European Champion
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Remco Evenepoel, crashes, recovers, attacks, does all the work and finally pips Ciccone in photo finish.
items.lbText:
Remco Evenepoel beats Giulio Ciccone to become European road race champion in Sencur, Slovenia. (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski/Getty Images) (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski)

Remco Evenepoel found redemption after a disappointing road race at the world championships, becoming European road race champ for the first time in his pro career after a dramatic finale.

The Belgian outsprinted Giulio Ciccone (Italy) at the line but had to wait for the result of a photo finish to confirm the win. Ciccone got a better line through the last corner and opened a lead of several bike lengths, but lost out by a tiny margin.

Evenepoel was fueled by pride and stubbornness, being determined to show well after his worlds disappointment and going into hulk mode after he went clear with Ciccone on the penultimate lap but crashed.

He took an uphill bend too fast and lost his front wheel, with his Belgian team keeping him within range and enabling him to jump up to Ciccone once again.

The Italian declined to work on the final lap, taking only one brief turn near the finish, and took the final corner better.

This gave him an important gap over Evenepoel but the Belgian wouldn’t be denied, chasing furiously all the way to the line and then lunging past. His throw to the line was better than that of Ciccone and this was just enough to give him the victory.

Christian Scaroni raced in 59 seconds back to make it an Italian silver and bronze, while Toms Skujiņš (Lavia) leap clear of a chase group to nab fourth, 1:13 back and three seconds ahead of Iván Romeo (Spain) and others.

Evenepoel was lucky not to be too affected by his fall. “It was a bit of a tricky situation the second last time on the climb. I put a nice attack but I went a bit too fast in the corner and I just slipped away,” he said.

“I think there I could have gone, but in the end we stayed calm and we came back to the plan. Then I put in an attack just before the descent and then I was with Cicco in the front.

“We worked together pretty well. The sprint was looking a bit…I thought I was not going to get it anymore, but then I saw him slowing down quite a lot with 100 meters to go and I just came just over him on the finish line.”

Evenepoel won the junior European road race championships in 2018 but this was his first time to take the distinctive blue and white jersey as a pro.

He took the time trial twice, in 2019 and 2025.

The elite men’s road race was 197km in distance and, like the women’s race, featured a mostly flat opening section of 85km prior to the start of the finishing circuit. The men would complete five laps compared to the women’s two, with the climb of Možjanca the main obstacle.

Six riders went clear very early on and had over a minute the first time over the finish line, but they were all caught with 82km remaining. The climb saw a large number of riders dropped from the peloton, including Juan Ayuso (Spain), and the contenders continued to dwindle with each passing lap.

Roglič’s Slovenia team took control of the pace the penultimate time up the climb but rather than the multiple Vuelta winner attacking, it was instead Giulio Ciccone (Italy) who leaped clear on with 36.3km remaining.

Evenepoel joined him almost immediately and then went past, launching a very aggressive surge, but went too fast into a right hand curve and lost the front wheel, crashing.

Ciccone went over the summit alone, chased by Roglič, while behind Evenepoel’s Belgium team were chasing hard and kept the Italian leader within range. He subsequently jumped clear and got up to Ciccone, with the two of them 12 seconds ahead of a group of chasers with 25km left.

Those behind trying to get across included Roglič, Toms Skujiņš (Latvia), Emil Herzog (Germany), Iván Romeo (Spain), Evenpoel’s teammates Ramses Debruyne and Maxim Van Gils, French trio Léo Bisiaux, Manhys Rondel and Clément Braz Afonso plus Christian Scaroni (Italy).

Roglič was under pressure as the home rider and did a lot of the chasing, but these were 26 seconds behind starting the final lap.

Rondel and Scaroni leaped clear in pursuit but with Evenepoel setting the pace out front the whole way up the climb, those two chasers were almost a minute back.

Scaroni attacked Rondel close to the summit in an attempt to bridge. Evenepoel was on a mission, though, and he had no chance of bridging. However there was still an advantage as once this information was passed on from a race moto, Ciccone made clear to Evenepoel that he couldn’t contribute. The Belgian wasn’t happy but continued driving onwards, hoping to win the sprint.

Ciccone finally started to ride inside the final 3km, making the decision after his team car drew alongside. However his contribution was minimal, with the Italian clearly trying to stay as fresh as possible.

Evenepoel led into the final corner but Ciccone got a better line and came past him. He launched early, opened several lengths, but Evenepoel chased hard all the way to the line and took the photo finish.

items.title: Evenepoel Hoping for Better at Euro Champs: ‘I Wouldn’t Say I’m Out for Revenge’
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Belgian star Remco Evenepoel aiming to bounce back from what was a difficult, confidence-shaking world championship ride
items.lbText:
Remco Evenepoel in action during the elite men's Road Race race at the cycling World Championships (Photo: Jasper Jacobs/Belga Mag via AFP) (Photo: JASPER JACOBS)

Second to Tadej Pogačar last year, Remco Evenepoel has one goal in mind for Sunday’s European championships : to win.

The Belgian has already won many of the big one day races he has been targeting in the sport: he was road world champion in 2022, Olympic champion in 2024, has won TTs at the same level and has clocked up two editions of Liège-Bastogne-Liège and four of the Clasica San Sebastian.

He’s a winner, and Sunday’s mission is to triumph.

There’s a problem though: his performance last weekend in the road worlds.

Evenepoel had looked supreme in the time trial seven days earlier, and also dominated the GP Cycliste de Québec. But his form deserted him when it was most needed, with things simply not working out in the road worlds.

It is, he said, something that will spur him on.

“I wouldn’t say I’m out for revenge, but I was definitely a bit disappointed that I wasn’t at the appointment,” he stated, referring to what was one of the biggest goals of his this season.

“It’s definitely been in my head over the last few days.”

When both Evenepoel and Belgium teammate Wout van Aert failed to perform at their best level in Montréal rumors went around that they were sick. That presumption was furthered in part by the illnesses of Lore De Schepper, Fleur Moors and Lotte Claes of the Belgian team.

Evenepoel was quick to quash those suggestions in the pre-Europeans press conference held on Friday evening.

“No, no… Don’t start, hey,” he smiled when asked if he had a cold.

“I’m not sick,” he said, according to Sporza .

“Everything had gone well in the run-up to that road race, but in the end it was just a bad day in terms of feeling,” he continued.

“The intensity training in the days beforehand went well. But now I just have to switch the button and try to ride a better race on Sunday.”

Montréal was a bigger challenge for Evenepoel.

Although last year’s winner Tadej Pogačar was absent, strong riders like Paul Seixas, Isaac Del Toro, Mathieu van der Poel, Tom Pidcock and others were present.

Each of those riders will be absent from the European championships, as will US competitors such as Matteo Jorgenson and eventual winner Brandon McNulty.

The field is less stacked and that could work in his favor, provided the race is hard enough.

He’ll be keen to put the worlds disappointment behind him. He’ll also be spurred on by the thoughts of winning the European road race title for the first time.

“That’s a big motivation for me,” Evenepoel confirmed. “The urge to do it is certainly present. That was actually the case last year, but it didn’t work out then.”

The issue then was Pogačar, who dominated the race. But the Slovenian champion is absent this time around due to injury, which removes one major challenger.

Several of those other rivals from the worlds will also be missing, but there are still strong riders to contend with.

One big concern is the Italian Giulio Ciccone. “He is really in good shape and will definitely compete for the win,” he said. Primož Roglič is another. “He was good at Montreal and will be motivated for his own audience,’ he said, referring to the championships being held in Roglič’s native Slovenia.

What’s crucial is that Evenepoel performs at his best on Sunday.

He said the shift in time zones from Canada made things a little trickier and that he still felt the effect on Tuesday. However by Wednesday he said his usual rhythm had returned.

“The training has gone pretty well, so I hope everything goes in a positive line towards Sunday now,” he said.

If it does, he will certainly be right up there.

Canada didn’t work out well but Slovenia might.

items.title: Piganzoli Scoops Giro Dell’Emilia as McNulty Debuts Rainbow Jersey
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Matteo Jorgenson plays vital role once again in teammate's success, just one week after helping Brandon McNulty to win worlds.
items.lbText:
Davide Piganzoli (Visma-Lease a Bike) leads world champ Brandon McNulty (UAE Team Emirates - XRG) during the Giro dell'Emilia 2026 (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images) (Photo: @DarioBelingheri/@GettyImages)

Davide Piganzoli ran out the surprise winner of the Giro dell’Emilia on Saturday, benefiting from the same dedicated teamwork from Matteo Jorgenson that Brandon McNulty enjoyed at last weekend’s world championships.

Just as he did for McNulty, Jorgenson proved the kingmaker for Visma-Lease a Bike teammate Piganzoli after he launched a perfectly-timed solo attack in the finale.

The Italian made his move on a downhill with 4.8km to go, quickly gaining time while Jorgenson sat on wheels and marked all attempts to chase.

He started the final ascent of the San Luca climb with a 41 second lead and gave it everything on the 2.1km ascent, with Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5 Pro Cycling), Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos) and Ben Healy (EF Education EasyPost) all being marked by Jorgenson.

Pidcock leaped clear closer to the line and narrowed the gap to just two seconds, with Onley taking third. Jorgenson was fifth, 12 seconds back, while McNulty had a solid showing in his first outing in the rainbow jersey with tenth.

“I picked the right moment to attack, and it paid off,” Piganzoli said afterward. “We had several cards to play. We handled this race perfectly as a team. It means a lot to me to add this great race to my palmares.”

Although he won the recent Tour de Luxembourg, he looked far from the strongest on the penultimate ascent of the climb.

Jorgenson made his move there with 10.5km remaining, close to the summit, and went solo. Ben Healy (EF Education-EasyPost) brought back him before the top, with Onley also there, and on the descent they were joined by Pidcock and Piganzoli.

The latter made his move with 4.8km remaining, choosing the perfect moment. With Jorgenson blocking, he gained enough time to hold on until the end.

“I felt good in the closing kilometers, so I decided to go all in,” Piganzoli said. “I also wanted to put my teammates in a good position that way. We still had Ben behind us, who has a strong sprint.

“In the end, I was able to finish it off myself, but this was a victory for the entire team. I’m happy that I was able to show my good form from Luxembourg and the world championships here again.”

Saturday was the first chance for McNulty to show off his rainbow jersey and rainbow-adorned bike since his surprise win in last weekend’s world championships.

The steep gradients of the San Luca climb didn’t play to his strengths but he rode aggressively, going briefly clear with 19km to go and later remaining close to the lighter riders when they went all in with one lap to go. He ended up in the second chasing group on the road.

McNulty has made clear winning the worlds won’t prevent him from riding for team leader Tadej Pogačar and others, but he certainly performed strongly on Saturday. He eventually finished tenth, 45 seconds behind Piganzoli.

“Today was really special, racing in the rainbow jersey for the first time, and I enjoyed every moment of it,” he said afterwards.

“I gave everything last weekend at the world championships, so I knew I might still be missing a little bit today.

“It was a tough day out there, but there are still plenty of opportunities to come and I’m looking forward to the next races.”

McNulty is scheduled to ride the Coppa Agostoni on Sunday and then Tre Valli Varesine on Tuesday.

He is also expected to line out in Il Lombardia next Saturday, as is an in-form Jorgenson.

items.title: Dream Season Continues as New World Champ Vollering Defends European Title
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Demi Vollering is too strong once again, soloing to second consecutive European champs victory.
items.lbText:
Demi Vollering (Netherlands) wins the European road championships on October 03, 2026 in Sencur, Slovenia. (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski/Getty Images) (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski)

One week after becoming world champion for the first time, Demi Vollering has doubled up with the European champs jersey, successfully defending the title she won last year.

Vollering continued a dream season with an assertive solo performance, going clear on the final lap with worlds runner-up Kasia Niewiadoma (Poland) and her own Dutch teammate Puck Pieterse. They dropped the other favorites on the Možjanca climb, with Vollering then kicking clear alone with just under 15km remaining.

Niewiadoma chased hard but with Pieterse sitting on, the duo were 34 seconds back with 12.2km to go. They were joined by Elisa Longo Borghini (Italy) and Antonia Niedermaier (Germany), with Marlen Reusser (Switzerland) bridging soon afterwards.

That gave the chasers numerical advantage but Vollering was too powerful, driving onwards towards the finish and notching up yet another win in what is a stunning season.

“It is really a golden year,” she said. “It is sad it is already over. Only the TT, and then it is off season already. But I cannot wait to race next year all year in this jersey and hopefully have a good season again.”

Niewiadoma crashed towards the finish, losing any chance of a medal. Pieterse won the sprint for second, five seconds back, with Reusser and Longo Borghini third and fourth. Niedermaier was 15 seconds adrift while a disappointed Niewiadoma limped in 45 seconds behind.

She will rue losing the chance to go for a medal, but Vollering was clearly a class above everyone.

“I just really love winning and it never gets boring for me,” she said, making clear that she still has many dreams in the sport.

“I think also it is not only the winning for me, but just proving yourself and getting better every day. Working on yourself every day and seeing what is still possible for the future. I think that is what I love most about this job.”

The elite women’s road race had a very different course to that of last week’s world road championship. The course in Montréal was very draining but Saturday’s 130km event in Slovenia was primarily flat for the first two thirds. However, following the start of two finishing laps, things did get more difficult.

The riders would face the Možjanca climb on each of those laps and while it was just 2.1km in length, it averaged 10.4 percent.

The days break saw Carina Schrempf (Austria) and Margot Vanpachtenbeke (Belgium) go clear less than 10km from the start and remain out front until 39km to go. The first ascent of the climb saw Reusser surge with 35km to go and force a group clear containing the world champion Vollering, Pieterse, Longo Borghini, Niedermaier, Niewiadoma and Juliette Berthet (France).

However while these are all very powerful riders, the terrain enabled a large regrouping on and after the descent.

Franziska Koch (Germany) and Cecilie Uttrup Ludwig (Denmark) then played their hand with 28km remaining. They got 25 seconds but were gobbled up with 19km left, just before Liane Lippert (Germany) attacked on a ramp and was joined by Noemi Rüegg (Switzerland) and Femke De Vries (Netherlands).

That trio sped towards the climb with a lead of 20 seconds but were reeled in with 16km remaining. Vollering, Pieterse and Niewiadoma pushed forward on the uphill but when the world champion surged with just under 15km remaining, she quickly moved clear.

Niewiadoma chased, with Pieterse sitting on, and while Longo Borghini, Niedermaier and Reusser rejoined, that collective strength could do nothing against Vollering.

She was well able to hold them off, racing to her second major triumph in eight days.

items.title: ‘Larry! Larry!’: Fans Give Warbasse Royal Treatment in Historic USA Worlds Win
items.author: ahood
items.content: As Team USA’s road captain, Larry Warbasse helped others chase gold. Then Montréal’s fans gave him a moment he’ll never forget.
items.lbText:
Warbasse got a rousing reception in Montréal during the 2026 road worlds. (Photo: Andrej Ivanov / AFP)

Larry Warbasse had taken his pulls and was riding to the finish at the UCI Road World Championships when the fans started an impromptu homage to the popular American.

On the final laps of the world championships in Montréal, the U.S. road captain climbed through a crowd that tipped their collective hats to the 36-year-old.

Up the road, Brandon McNulty was racing toward the rainbow jersey.

Behind, Warbasse was getting a royal reception of his own for a job well done in America’s first elite men’s road title in 33 years .

“Yeah, even the last couple of laps I was dropped and I don’t know who started it, but they started just chanting like Larry! Larry!,” Warbasse told Velo . “Like the whole way up the climb, so that was pretty cool.”

McNulty’s Montréal worlds win was a collective effort for Team USA , and Warbasse played a special role during the race and behind the scenes.

As the designated road captain, he helped position and protect the American leaders until crunch time in the closing laps in the squad’s rainbow jersey-winning tactics .

“I thought with my experience and the years in the peloton, I could play a vital role,” he said. “I really wanted to race this worlds because I knew we’d have a super strong team.”

Warbasse had Montréal circled on his calendar ever since it was announced. It was the first North American worlds since Richmond in 2015.

He knew the Americans were assembling an unusually strong team, and he wanted to be there.

McNulty, Matteo Jorgenson, and Quinn Simmons would lead. Warbasse wanted to bring his experience to help them succeed.

“For me it was it was a huge honor just to even be there,” he said. “A lot of those guys have been racing together since they were juniors. I’m a little older but I know these guys from racing together and we had a really good vibe the whole week. It was just a group of American buddies.”

The unique bond helped McNulty and the team to pull of the miracle in Montréal.

A pro since 2012, Warbasse was the most experienced rider on the team of America’s golden generation .

“I was the road captain and my job was to make sure everyone was in the right position and be aware of the race situation,” Warbasse told Velo .

“Earlier in the race I was speaking with some of the other teams, trying to figure what’s going to happen. The race opened up pretty far out and I tried to stay there as long as possible.”

Warbasse said Montréal’s relentless succession of climbs and descents meant it wasn’t easy to stay together on the circuit.

Everyone had a solid game plan going into the finale, and despite racing without race radios, when the moves went down, everyone had a tactical blueprint to follow.

With the race going off ahead of him , Warbasse dug deep to stay in the race in case something happened.

And then something magical did start to happen. Fans spotted Warbasse and started calling out his name.

It’s a phenomenon that’s been growing the past few years, with fans cheering for riders like Wout Van Aert as they roll past. Warbasse is now part of that orbit.

Warbasse — who is set to race in 2027 with Tudor Pro Cycling — called it the coolest race he had done in North America.

“There were so many people on all the climbs. It was a wall of noise every time you went up each of the climbs,” he said. “It was pretty insane, a really, really nice atmosphere.”

Writing on Instagram, he said how much the impromptu love session meant to him.

“To all of the fans who somehow spread my name up and down every single climb on the route and chanted my name each time we went past, it felt like I was the one who won in the end,” Warbasse said. “I had goosebumps the whole way, and nearly had tears in my eyes feeling all the love.”

The fans also helped him follow what was happening up the road.

“All the people on the side of the road were giving me updates and when I came through, I could see on the jumbotron that Brandon was up the road,” Warbasse told Velo .

“Then once he won, everyone was going crazy. When I heard that he won, I was a bit speechless and I was just so excited.”

The celebration continued with dinner and a night out, a small gathering of teammates and a few friends. They celebrated the historical victory in one of the best worlds in recent years .

Back in Europe to close out the season with Tudor, Warbasse said he appreciated how rare it is for a rider to share a moment like that with his compatriots.

“Maybe that’s the only time in your life you get to be a part of such a huge victory,” he said. “I’ll definitely remember this one for a long time.”

items.title: Like Day and Night: the Two New World Champ Bikes Take Opposite Approaches to the Rainbow Stripes
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: We dove into the two new rainbow bikes from Colnago and Specialized, as well as a short look back at our favorite rainbow bikes of the past few years.
items.lbText:
It’s been just under a week since the 2026 UCI Road World Championships, and the paint shops at Colnago and Specialized have been hard at work.

To celebrate the two new elite world champions, Brandon McNulty and Demi Vollering, the champions’ bike sponsors have been hard at work to deliver them two unique liveries for the next year of racing. Interestingly, despite the two design teams working from the classic black, white, and rainbow color scheme, the two iconic brands have created dramatically different designs.
